newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn sees no reason to change forex stance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn sees no reason to change forex stance.

text.p: The German government said on Wednesday speculators were behind the dollar's recent rise and that Bonn had no reason to change its currency market stance.
No sign of central bank intervention has been seen from Germany or elsewhere despite an accelerating climb that has taken the dollar to 1.89 marks, its highest level since 1989.

While Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer have in recent weeks said they are unhappy with the dollar's gains, the Bundesbank has done no more than indicate it could begin to nudge market interest rates higher.
But market participants say that would not be enough to bolster the mark, and the dollar is showing no sign of stopping.
While worries about European monetary union are hobbling the mark, the dollar is gaining due to a strong U.S. economy and expectations of a possible increase in U.S. interest rates, they said.
"The dollar's recent strength is due to strong speculative impulses," government spokesman Peter Hausmann told a news conference. "The government sees no reason to change its stance."
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet has not held any special discussions on the subject of the dollar's value against the mark recently, Hausmann said.
A finance ministry spokeswoman said little has changed since the February meeting in Berlin of finance ministers from the Group of Seven major industrialised nations.

At that meeting, when the dollar had rebounded to about 1.65 marks from 1.35 marks in two years ago, the ministers said the correction of the dollar's previous weakness was largely complete and that the dollar's value should reflect economic fundamentals.
The ministers never mentioned particular measures or dollar levels, the spokeswoman said.
Last month Waigel and Tietmeyer said they thought the dollar rise had been overdone when it topped 1.80 marks.

Waigel hinted there could be G7 central bank intervention, by saying that Germany was in contact with its G7 partners, but this has not been followed up by any coordinated action to stem the dollar's rise.
